text: Now that you can load a DataFrame three different ways, the next skill is pulling exactly what you need out of one — specific columns, specific rows matching a condition, and specific rows by label.

df of customer_name with single brackets gives you back a Series — one column. Wrap the column names in a second set of brackets, like order_id, product, quantity, and you get a smaller DataFrame instead. That one extra bracket trips people up constantly.

df of quantity less than zero produces a True-False Series, one value per row, and feeding that straight back into df brackets keeps only the rows where it's True. This finds order 1014's negative quantity in one line — the same row you found manually back in Chapter 3.

To combine conditions, wrap each one in its own parentheses and join them with ampersand for and, or pipe for or. Skip the parentheses and Python's operator precedence will give you a confusing error, because bare equals-equals next to ampersand doesn't parse the way you'd expect.

set_index swaps the default 0, 1, 2 index for order_id itself, so dot-loc of 1005 means the row labeled 1005 — not position 1005. Notice customer_name prints as NaN here: that's pandas' way of showing a missing value, and Lesson 22 deals with it properly.

You now know how to slice a DataFrame down to exactly what matters. Next lesson tackles this dataset's two real problems head-on: filling in that missing customer name, and a duplicate-detection trap waiting in the customer_name column.
